newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says Russia will meet Alpha targets.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says Russia will meet Alpha targets.

text.p: Russia was on target to finish building its part of an international space station on time, President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday.
He also signed a decree sanctioning the raising of nearly $100 million in foreign investment this year to provide extra funds to ensure construction of the Alpha space station goes smoothly.

"All problems in building the Russian part of the station have been solved, including financial questions. The construction is going according to schedule," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.

Yeltsin said he had also spoken to U.S. President Bill Clinton about this two months ago. "I have reassured him down, in any case we will finish not later than they (U.S constructors) will," Yeltsin said in televised remarks.
He made his comments during a visit to the Khrunichev space centre in Moscow which is building some of the parts for Alpha, the next generation of space stations after Russia's ageing Mir.

Russia finished the first module for Alpha, which is to be completed by the year 2003, months behind schedule. The delay produced protests from the United States and other foreign participants who said the entire project might be in jeopardy.
Moscow is due to finish the second module, the crew's accommodation, by December, 1998.

The Russian government promised in April to come up with more funds to ensure the construction is completed. By May, it had provided 800 billion ($138 milion) of the 1.5 trillion roubles ($260 million) pledged by issuing promissory notes.

In the second stage of this fund-raising, Yeltsin signed a decree on Friday permitting the finance ministry to raise $99.5 million from foreign banks to fund Russia's involvement in Alpha. The text of the decree was released by the Kremlin.

The Russian Space Agency has said Russia's work on 12 of Alpha's 36 modules will cost $3.2 billion. The United States plans to build 18 modules worth $17.2 billion. The European Space Agency, Japan, Canada and Italy are also contributing.
A Russian space official said on Thursday the Russian Space Agency needed about 5.3 trillion roubles ($910 million) from the state budget to fund its entire space programme in 1998.
Yeltsin said it would be impossible to determine what had caused a string of problems on Mir until after the crew which encountered them returned to Earth on August 14.

"Specialists have said that at first glance it was not due to technical failure and that apparently the human factor played a part, although it is impossible to say for sure," Russian television pictures showed Yeltsin saying.

A module collided with Mir on June 25 in the worst accident in the space station's history. It has had power and oxygen supply problems since then, one crew member developed a heart problem and an unidentified liquid leaked into space.
